title: Mapping Colombia's Revived Caribbean Cocaine Corridors
summary: Maya and Daniel dissect a comprehensive report from the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) on how Colombian cocaine trafficking routes through the Caribbean are reviving to supply booming European markets. They explore the internal transport corridors, maritime smuggling methods, corruption dynamics, and regional geopolitical shifts detailed in the investigation.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Welcome to our briefing. Today we're looking at a fascinating new report published by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, or GI-TOC. It is titled 'Colombia: Caribbean Routes Revive as Cocaine Flows Shift Towards European Markets', written by Lina María Asprilla and Andrés Aponte.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And if you follow international drug trafficking, Latin American security, or European illicit markets, this is essential reading. For years, Pacific routes dominated the headlines. But this report lays out how Colombia's Caribbean coastline is seeing a massive revival as a strategic launchpad.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Right. The authors note that while the US market has long been the primary destination, it's increasingly saturated with tightened controls. Meanwhile, demand in Europe has surged. In 2025, an estimated 4.6 million people in Europe aged 15 to 64 reported consuming cocaine. Wastewater data reflects doubling and tripling rates in places like France and Germany.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And that massive European pull is reshaping the logistics chain inside Colombia. Let's start with production, because the report begins with some eye-opening numbers on just how much coca Colombia is producing right now.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It's staggering. Potential cocaine production in Colombia has tripled over the last two decades. Cultivation expanded from around 160,000 hectares to 261,000 hectares. But what's crucial is that even as production exploded, the geographic concentration remained heavily clustered. Five main production zones feed this Caribbean corridor: Catatumbo in Norte de Santander, Sur de Bolívar, Bajo Cauca in Antioquia, Putumayo, and Sur de Córdoba.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And despite the huge volumes being seized—the report mentions over 550 tonnes intercepted nationally between 2020 and 2024—experts cited in the study point out pure cocaine production is growing much faster than the state's capacity to intercept it. In 2023, potential production jumped 53%, meaning seizures actually represented a smaller fraction of the total output.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. Seizures hit records, but supply outpaced them. The report also highlights the shifting political backdrop. Under former President Gustavo Petro, policy prioritized interdiction over forced eradication. But mounting tensions with Washington, leading to Colombia being decertified, culminated in a sharp political shift in the 2026 elections with President Abelardo de la Espriella taking power.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Who is pivoting right back toward forced eradication and heavy military alignment with the US, including joining the Shield of the Americas initiative. But as the report warns, cracking down on producers and transporters without addressing structural poverty rarely stops the flows.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Which brings us directly to how the drugs move from those inland coca enclaves up to the Caribbean coast. The report traces four distinct internal transit corridors, and the criminal dynamics along each are really complex.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Let's unpack that. In the western zone, Sur de Córdoba and Bajo Cauca, who dominates the routes?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: In the west, it's overwhelmingly the EGC—the Ejército Gaitanista de Colombia, also known as the Clan del Golfo. In Sur de Córdoba, they control the entire chain: cultivation, processing, and transit. Cocaine moves out of Nudo de Paramillo along the Sinú river or via national highways like Routes 21, 23, and 74 toward the Gulf of Urabá and coastal towns like Moñitos, San Bernardo del Viento, and San Antero.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Though interestingly, field interviews revealed that the river route down the Sinú has fallen out of favor over the last two years because security forces stepped up patrols and seizures. So the EGC adapted, shifting traffic eastward through places like Planeta Rica and across the wetlands of La Mojana toward Cartagena and the Gulf of Morrosquillo.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: That's their playbook: adaptability. Along the highways, the report notes the EGC evades police using networks of lookouts, local corruption, and the fact that highway police simply lack technical tools like advanced scanners for freight trucks. But while the EGC has near-monopoly control in Córdoba and parts of Bajo Cauca, the picture in the eastern Caribbean is completely different.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Right, because in Sur de Bolívar and Catatumbo, you have violent fragmentation. In Sur de Bolívar, the EGC is locked in a fierce territorial dispute with the ELN and FARC dissident factions, fighting over coca, mobility corridors, and illegal gold mining.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: And in Catatumbo, right on the border with Venezuela, the historic truce between the ELN and FARC dissidents like Frente 33 has fractured into open war. On top of that, a regional group based around Santa Marta—the ACSN, or Autodefensas Conquistadoras de la Sierra Nevada—has tried pushing into Catatumbo to secure its own supply lines and avoid paying transit fees to the EGC.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And that conflict explains why routes to the eastern coast—through Cesar into Magdalena and La Guajira—are so volatile. Without a single dominant hegemon like the EGC in the west, alliances are unstable, lookouts can't be maintained as easily, and river transport down the Magdalena River becomes critical.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Once the shipments hit the coast, how does the cocaine actually leave Colombia? The report breaks maritime trafficking down into two major arenas: public commercial ports, and the vast network of informal, alternative natural ports.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Let's look at the commercial container ports first. The Caribbean handles over 85% of Colombia's maritime freight. And the crown jewel is Cartagena.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Gran Puerto de Cartagena is massive—the best-connected port in Latin America and the Caribbean, connecting to around 150 countries. Between 2021 and 2025, it registered the highest number of drug seizures in the country, ahead of Santa Marta and Barranquilla. It has direct maritime lines to major European entry points like Rotterdam, Antwerp, Hamburg, and several ports in France and Italy.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the methods used to exploit these ports are fascinating. It's not just shoving bags into containers. The report describes systematic contamination. Banana exports are the primary target—they represent Colombia's top agricultural export to the EU, and because bananas are perishable, cargo has to move through port inspections rapidly. In early 2025 alone, banana exports jumped 22%, expanding the concealment window.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Coal is another major cover. The report mentions a 2023 seizure in Barranquilla of nearly two and a half tonnes of cocaine disguised as coal bound for Belgium. Because coal moves on smaller bulk vessels that can dock at shallower, secondary European ports with less oversight, it offers a distinct logistical advantage.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Then there are the divers. The so-called 'parasite technique', where divers attach waterproof metal canisters containing cocaine directly to ship hulls beneath the waterline before the vessels leave port or while at sea. The report notes that in 2021, an outfit called Troya was broken up after allegedly moving more than 20 tonnes to Europe this way through Barranquilla, Cartagena, and Santa Marta.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: And who is coordinating this inside the port cities? The report brings up an intriguing finding from field interviews in Santa Marta about an entity locally known as 'La Oficina'. It's described as a quiet consortium of influential traditional families with decades-long ties to trafficking, using municipal leverage and private coastal properties to broker logistics for multiple armed groups, connecting them with Italian and European mafias. Though, as the authors note, there's virtually no public records or official cases documenting them.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Meanwhile, the violence in port cities like Barranquilla and Santa Marta has spiked as local outfits like Los Costeños clash with the EGC and ACSN for control of access roads, warehouses, and river mouths where drug shipments converge.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Beyond the big commercial terminals, though, the real workhorse of the Caribbean revival is the network of natural and informal ports. Beaches, estuaries, mangrove swamps stretching across the Gulf of Morrosquillo, Urabá, and especially La Alta Guajira.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: This is where go-fast boats operate. They're built from fibreglass and carbon fibre with multiple high-powered outboards, carrying between one and five tonnes. But the report also points out recent technological leaps: in July 2025, the Colombian navy seized an unmanned, remote-controlled semi-submersible being tested by the EGC off Santa Marta.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: And to avoid detection, traffickers aren't just using sheltered bays anymore. They've started launching directly from exposed ocean beaches with rough surf and minimal tourist or police presence. But what struck me most in this section was the human dimension—the deep reliance on local coastal communities.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: That was one of the most sobering parts of the report. In places like Villa Fátima in Riohacha, or Rincón del Mar in San Onofre, extreme poverty and state absence have completely normalized participation in the drug economy. Local youth work as boat builders, mechanics, or sailors.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: In Villa Fátima, a community of about 400 families, the report notes that at least 42 residents are currently incarcerated in foreign prisons abroad, and 12 have disappeared at sea. Yet when a young man can earn up to 15 times a normal monthly wage in a single run, the economic calculus drives them right back into the trade. Wealthy local financiers even back these trips for massive returns.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Now let's zoom out to the broader international connections, because once these boats launch from Colombia, where do they go? The report identifies three pivotal transit nodes: Venezuela, the Dominican Republic, and Central America.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Let's touch on Venezuela first. The report notes two major exit pathways through Venezuela. One goes through the Orinoco and Venezuelan Amazon, using clandestine airstrips to fly cocaine out to Suriname, Guyana, and the Lesser Antilles. The other moves from Catatumbo into Zulia, Falcón, and Carabobo, feeding maritime departures.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the authors note that the ELN has developed a very specific cross-border corridor in Alta Guajira. By cracking down on highway robbery along Venezuela's Cojoro highway, the ELN won the cooperation of local Wayuu clans, allowing them to bypass Colombian military checkpoints and run cocaine directly into Venezuelan territory and out by boat.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: There are direct maritime links from Venezuela to Europe, too. In late 2024, Spanish authorities seized over 3.3 tonnes of cocaine off the Canary Islands from a Venezuelan fishing vessel. And shipments from Guyana have even utilized trans-Atlantic semi-submersibles heading straight for Spain.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Then there is the Dominican Republic, which the report describes as having taken on an unprecedented role since the pandemic. Alta Guajira is less than 450 nautical miles from the Dominican coast.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Right, and Dominican boatmen have become the elite transporters for this route. They know the navigation, they know the Dominican unloading zones, and they can command fees up to 300 million Colombian pesos—about 70,000 euros—for a single trip. The report notes that Dominican networks have established strong footprints in Europe, especially Spain, as demonstrated by the major takedown of the Rostetan gang in Operation Búfalo NK in late 2025.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And on the other side of the Atlantic, who is receiving all this? The report documents extensive infiltration by European organized crime operating directly inside Colombia. High-ranking operatives from the Italian 'Ndrangheta, the Camorra, and the Balkan cartel have been arrested in cities like Barranquilla, Medellín, Cartagena, and Cali.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: They aren't just buying shipments at European docks anymore; they're on the ground in Colombia financing shipments, organizing maritime freight logistics, and laundering profits in partnership with groups like the EGC. It's a completely integrated global supply chain.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: So when you look at all of this—the record production, the adaptable inland routes, the coopted ports, the island waypoints—what does the GI-TOC recommend policymakers do?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: The authors emphasize that pure interdiction and crop eradication have demonstrably failed to dismantle these networks. First, for producing areas, they call for comprehensive rural development and viable economic alternatives to break the structural dependence on coca.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Second, along internal transport corridors, they urge Colombia to upgrade police technical capacities—cargo scanners, non-intrusive inspection arches, and intelligent weighbridges on trunk roads—backed by rigorous counterintelligence to weed out corruption within the security forces.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Third, on port security, Colombia still lacks a dedicated, coordinated national strategy against maritime smuggling. The report urges expanding initiatives like the European Ports Alliance, building direct bilateral ties between ports like Antwerp, Rotterdam, Hamburg, and their Colombian counterparts, and deepening EU cooperation through mechanisms like El PAcCTO and COPOLAD.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And finally, for the coastal communities, security crackdowns cannot be the only answer. Interventions must offer real livelihood alternatives, infrastructure, and basic public services to rebuild trust and strip away the economic necessity that makes trafficking the only game in town.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: As we look ahead, the big things to watch will be how the de la Espriella administration's return to forced eradication plays out on the ground, whether port automation can outpace cartel corruption, and how European law enforcement handles the unrelenting flow of cocaine through the Caribbean corridor.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: A critical report on a rapidly shifting illicit trade. The full publication from GI-TOC is available on their website. Thanks for tuning in.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: See you next time.
